claim: Cryptosporidium is responsible for diarrheal disease in young children causing death, malnutrition, and growth delay.
source: The parasite Cryptosporidium is responsible for diarrheal disease in young children causing death, malnutrition, and growth delay.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge about Cryptosporidium pathogenesis.

claim: Cryptosporidium invades enterocytes where it develops in a unique intracellular niche.
source: Cryptosporidium invades enterocytes where it develops in a unique intracellular niche.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of Cryptosporidium infection.

claim: Infected cells exhibit profound changes in morphology, physiology, and transcriptional activity.
source: Infected cells exhibit profound changes in morphology, physiology, and transcriptional activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the RNA sequencing results.

claim: Members of the Cryptosporidium parvum MEDLE protein family are translocated into the cytosol of infected cells.
source: We explored the localization of highly polymorphic proteins and found members of the Cryptosporidium parvum MEDLE protein family to be translocated into the cytosol of infected cells.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by immunofluorescence assays and multiple transgenic parasite lines.

claim: All intracellular life stages of C. parvum engage in MEDLE2 export.
source: All intracellular life stages engage in this export, which occurs after completion of invasion.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments and stage-specific antibody staining shown in Figure 2.

claim: MEDLE2 export occurs after completion of invasion.
source: All intracellular life stages engage in this export, which occurs after completion of invasion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the timing experiments in Figure 3 showing MEDLE2 is not present in sporozoites but appears 4-5 hours post-invasion.

claim: MEDLE2 contains an N-terminal host-targeting motif.
source: Mutational studies defined an N-terminal host-targeting motif and demonstrated proteolytic processing at a specific leucine residue.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational analysis in Figure 5 showing that the KDVSLI motif and specifically leucine 35 are required for export.

claim: MEDLE2 undergoes proteolytic processing at a specific leucine residue.
source: Mutational studies defined an N-terminal host-targeting motif and demonstrated proteolytic processing at a specific leucine residue.
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blot analysis in Figure 5E-F showing size differences between wild-type and mutant proteins.

claim: Direct expression of MEDLE2 in mammalian cells triggered an ER stress response.
source: Direct expression of MEDLE2 in mammalian cells triggered an ER stress response, which was also observed during infection.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data from transfected HEK293T cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: An ER stress response was observed during C. parvum infection.
source: Direct expression of MEDLE2 in mammalian cells triggered an ER stress response, which was also observed during infection.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of published infection datasets and qPCR from infected mice shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: C. parvum has a secretion system capable of delivering parasite proteins into the infected enterocyte.
source: Taken together, our studies reveal the presence of a Cryptosporidium secretion system capable of delivering parasite proteins into the infected enterocyte.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective experimental evidence of MEDLE protein export.

claim: Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease worldwide.
source: The Apicomplexan parasite Cryptosporidium is a leading cause of diarrheal disease worldwide.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Young children are highly susceptible to Cryptosporidium infection.
source: Young children are highly susceptible to infection, and cryptosporidiosis is an important contributor to child mortality (Khalil et al., 2018; Kotloff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited epidemiological studies.

claim: Cryptosporidiosis is an important contributor to child mortality.
source: Young children are highly susceptible to infection, and cryptosporidiosis is an important contributor to child mortality (Khalil et al., 2018; Kotloff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited epidemiological studies.

claim: Children in resource-poor settings carry a disproportionate burden of severe cryptosporidiosis.
source: Children in resource-poor settings carry a disproportionate burden of severe disease (Choy and Huston, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Malnutrition enhances the risk of severe cryptosporidiosis.
source: Malnutrition enhances the risk of severe cryptosporidiosis, and at the same time, the disease impacts the nutritional state of children, which can lead to impaired growth (Costa et al., 2011; Mondal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Cryptosporidiosis impacts the nutritional state of children, which can lead to impaired growth.
source: Malnutrition enhances the risk of severe cryptosporidiosis, and at the same time, the disease impacts the nutritional state of children, which can lead to impaired growth (Costa et al., 2011; Mondal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Infection with Cryptosporidium results in protective immunity that is not sterile.
source: Infection with the parasite results in protective immunity, but this immunity is not sterile and may require multiple exposures to develop (Chappell et al., 1999; Okhuysen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited immunological studies.

claim: Protective immunity to Cryptosporidium may require multiple exposures to develop.
source: Infection with the parasite results in protective immunity, but this immunity is not sterile and may require multiple exposures to develop (Chappell et al., 1999; Okhuysen et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited immunological studies.

claim: Most human cryptosporidiosis is due to infection with Cryptosporidium hominis and Cryptosporidium parvum.
source: Most human diseases are due to infection with Cryptosporidium hominis, which only infects humans, and Cryptosporidium parvum, which can be zoonotically transmitted (Feng et al., 2018; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited epidemiological and genomic studies.

claim: Cryptosporidium hominis only infects humans.
source: Most human diseases are due to infection with Cryptosporidium hominis, which only infects humans, and Cryptosporidium parvum, which can be zoonotically transmitted (Feng et al., 2018; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about host specificity.

claim: Cryptosporidium parvum can be zoonotically transmitted.
source: Most human diseases are due to infection with Cryptosporidium hominis, which only infects humans, and Cryptosporidium parvum, which can be zoonotically transmitted (Feng et al., 2018; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transmission patterns.

claim: The emergence of Cryptosporidium species is driven by host adaptation resulting in specialization and narrowing host specificity.
source: The emergence of Cryptosporidium species is driven by host adaptation resulting in specialization and narrowing host specificity; however, the sexual life cycle of the parasite allows for recombination and can lead to rapid convergent evolution of host specificity (Guo et al., 2015; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited evolutionary and genomic studies.

claim: The sexual life cycle of Cryptosporidium allows for recombination and can lead to rapid convergent evolution of host specificity.
source: The emergence of Cryptosporidium species is driven by host adaptation resulting in specialization and narrowing host specificity; however, the sexual life cycle of the parasite allows for recombination and can lead to rapid convergent evolution of host specificity (Guo et al., 2015; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited evolutionary and genomic studies.

claim: Cryptosporidium infects the epithelium of the small intestine.
source: Cryptosporidium infects the epithelium of the small intestine, where it lives in a unique intracellular, but extracytoplasmic niche (Elliott and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the infection site.

claim: Cryptosporidium lives in a unique intracellular, but extracytoplasmic niche.
source: Cryptosporidium infects the epithelium of the small intestine, where it lives in a unique intracellular, but extracytoplasmic niche (Elliott and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the parasite's cellular location.

claim: The mechanism by which the Cryptosporidium intracellular niche is established during invasion involves rearrangement of the host actin cytoskeleton.
source: The mechanism by which this niche is established during invasion is still debated but involves the rearrangement of the host actin cytoskeleton, the formation of tight junction-like structures between host and parasite membranes, and a dense band of unknown composition at the host-parasite interphase (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on invasion mechanisms.

claim: The mechanism by which the Cryptosporidium intracellular niche is established involves the formation of tight junction-like structures between host and parasite membranes.
source: The mechanism by which this niche is established during invasion is still debated but involves the rearrangement of the host actin cytoskeleton, the formation of tight junction-like structures between host and parasite membranes, and a dense band of unknown composition at the host-parasite interphase (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on invasion mechanisms.

claim: The mechanism by which the Cryptosporidium intracellular niche is established involves a dense band of unknown composition at the host-parasite interphase.
source: The mechanism by which this niche is established during invasion is still debated but involves the rearrangement of the host actin cytoskeleton, the formation of tight junction-like structures between host and parasite membranes, and a dense band of unknown composition at the host-parasite interphase (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on invasion mechanisms.

claim: Cryptosporidium has severely reduced metabolic capabilities and relies heavily upon the host cell for nutrients and metabolites.
source: Cryptosporidium has severely reduced metabolic capabilities and relies heavily upon the host cell for nutrients and metabolites (Abrahamsen et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by cited genomic and metabolic studies.

claim: Many specialized uptake mechanisms in Cryptosporidium are believed to be localized to the feeder organelle at the host-parasite interface.
source: A number of specialized uptake mechanisms have been proposed to fill this need, many of which are believed to be localized to the so-called feeder organelle at the host-parasite interface (Guérin and Striepen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a cited review.

claim: Cryptosporidium remodels the host cell cytoskeleton.
source: In summary, Cryptosporidium remodels the host cell in significant ways that include its cytoskeleton (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000), cellular physiology and metabolism (Argenzio et al., 1990; Kumar et al., 2018), as well as aspects of immune restriction and regulation (Laurent and Lacroix-Lamandé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Cryptosporidium remodels host cellular physiology and metabolism.
source: In summary, Cryptosporidium remodels the host cell in significant ways that include its cytoskeleton (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000), cellular physiology and metabolism (Argenzio et al., 1990; Kumar et al., 2018), as well as aspects of immune restriction and regulation (Laurent and Lacroix-Lamandé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Cryptosporidium remodels aspects of host immune restriction and regulation.
source: In summary, Cryptosporidium remodels the host cell in significant ways that include its cytoskeleton (Bonnin et al., 1999; Elliott and Clark, 2000), cellular physiology and metabolism (Argenzio et al., 1990; Kumar et al., 2018), as well as aspects of immune restriction and regulation (Laurent and Lacroix-Lamandé, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Many bacterial, protozoan, and fungal pathogens use translocated effectors to manipulate their hosts.
source: Many bacterial, protozoan, and fungal pathogens use translocated effectors to manipulate their hosts to secure nutrients and to block host immunity.
evidence: This is general knowledge in the field of host-pathogen interactions.

claim: In Plasmodium falciparum, exported effectors form adhesive structures on the surface of red blood cells to alter tissue distribution and mechanical properties to prevent clearance.
source: In Plasmodium falciparum, exported effectors form adhesive structures on the surface of red blood cells to alter tissue distribution and mechanical properties to prevent clearance (Crabb et al., 1997; Leech et al., 1984) and install new nutrient and ion uptake mechanisms (Baumeister et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on P. falciparum.

claim: Plasmodium falciparum exported effectors install new nutrient and ion uptake mechanisms.
source: In Plasmodium falciparum, exported effectors form adhesive structures on the surface of red blood cells to alter tissue distribution and mechanical properties to prevent clearance (Crabb et al., 1997; Leech et al., 1984) and install new nutrient and ion uptake mechanisms (Baumeister et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on P. falciparum.

claim: In Toxoplasma gondii, translocated effectors disarm critical elements of interferon-induced cellular restriction.
source: In Toxoplasma gondii, translocated effectors disarm critical elements of interferon-induced cellular restriction (Gay et al., 2016; Olias et al., 2016), establish access to cellular nutrients, and rewire signaling and transcriptional networks to antagonize immune responses to promote a favorable environment for parasite growth (Bougdour et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2019; Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on T. gondii.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii translocated effectors establish access to cellular nutrients.
source: In Toxoplasma gondii, translocated effectors disarm critical elements of interferon-induced cellular restriction (Gay et al., 2016; Olias et al., 2016), establish access to cellular nutrients, and rewire signaling and transcriptional networks to antagonize immune responses to promote a favorable environment for parasite growth (Bougdour et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2019; Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on T. gondii.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii translocated effectors rewire signaling and transcriptional networks to antagonize immune responses.
source: In Toxoplasma gondii, translocated effectors disarm critical elements of interferon-induced cellular restriction (Gay et al., 2016; Olias et al., 2016), establish access to cellular nutrients, and rewire signaling and transcriptional networks to antagonize immune responses to promote a favorable environment for parasite growth (Bougdour et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2013; Braun et al., 2019; Gold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on T. gondii.

claim: Cryptosporidium has been hypothesized to use exported effector proteins to ensure its survival.
source: Cryptosporidium has been hypothesized to use exported effector proteins to ensure its survival (Pellé et al., 2015); however, to date, no such factors have been identified.
evidence: This is supported by a cited hypothesis, with the authors noting that prior to this study no such factors had been identified.

claim: Prior to this study, no exported effector proteins had been identified in Cryptosporidium.
source: Cryptosporidium has been hypothesized to use exported effector proteins to ensure its survival (Pellé et al., 2015); however, to date, no such factors have been identified.
evidence: This establishes the novelty of the current findings.

claim: MEDLE2 is exported to the host cell cytoplasm by all stages of the C. parvum life cycle in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here, we report that the polymorphic protein MEDLE2 is exported to the host cell cytoplasm by all stages of the C. parvum life cycle in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the time-course experiments in Figure 2 and in vivo imaging in Figure 2E.

claim: MEDLE2 is not injected during invasion, but rather is transported into the host cell following the initial establishment of infection.
source: This protein is not injected during invasion, but rather is transported into the host cell following the initial establishment of infection.
evidence: This is supported by the timing experiments in Figure 3 showing MEDLE2 is not present in sporozoites.

claim: MEDLE2 export requires a signal that includes a proteolytic cleavage site.
source: We carefully mapped the requirements for export and found a signal that includes a proteolytic cleavage site, and we demonstrate that exported proteins undergo processing.
evidence: This is supported by the mutational analysis and western blots in Figure 5.

claim: Exported MEDLE proteins undergo processing.
source: We carefully mapped the requirements for export and found a signal that includes a proteolytic cleavage site, and we demonstrate that exported proteins undergo processing.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot analysis in Figure 5E-F showing size differences.

claim: C. parvum has a robust translocation mechanism established by intracellular parasites that delivers parasite proteins to the host cell.
source: Overall, we demonstrate the presence of a robust translocation mechanism established by intracellular parasites that delivers parasite proteins to the host cell.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the collective experimental evidence.

claim: The C. parvum genome encodes multiple families of paralogous proteins that carry N-terminal signal peptides and share conserved amino acid repeat motifs.
source: The genome of C. parvum encodes multiple families of paralogous proteins that carry N-terminal signal peptides and share conserved amino acid repeat motifs among family members (Abrahamsen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a cited genomic study.

claim: Polymorphic gene families in C. parvum are often found within clusters located proximal to the telomeres of multiple chromosomes.
source: These genes are often found within clusters (homologous and heterologous), many of which are located proximal to the telomeres of multiple chromosomes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and is based on genomic analysis.

claim: Polymorphic genes in C. parvum are highly polymorphic and vary in copy number when comparing strains and species.
source: Comparing strains and species, these genes are highly polymorphic and vary in copy number, which has been interpreted as a sign of rapid evolution driven by their roles in invasion, pathogenesis, and host cell specificity (Guo et al., 2015; Nader et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by cited comparative genomic studies.

claim: The polymorphism and copy number variation of certain C. parvum genes has been interpreted as a sign of rapid evolution driven by their roles in invasion, pathogenesis, and host cell specificity.
source: Comparing strains and species, these genes are highly polymorphic and vary in copy number, which has been interpreted as a sign of rapid evolution driven by their roles in invasion, pathogenesis, and host cell specificity (Guo et al., 2015; Nader et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019)
evidence: This is an interpretation from cited studies.

claim: Selected polymorphic loci were modified in C. parvum IOWAII isolate using CRISPR/Cas9-driven homologous recombination to append three hemagglutinin epitopes.
source: Selected loci were modified in the C. parvum IOWAII isolate using CRISPR/Cas9-driven homologous recombination (Vinayak et al., 2015) to append three hemagglutinin epitopes (3XHA) in translational fusion to the C-terminus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used, with reference to the method citation.

claim: Drug-resistant parasites were recovered for four of six initial polymorphic gene candidates.
source: Drug-resistant parasites were recovered for four of six initial candidates, and successful genomic insertion was mapped by PCR (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the transgenic parasite generation.

claim: For most polymorphic gene candidates tested, the tagged protein appeared to coincide with the parasite and/or the parasitophorous vacuole.
source: For most candidates, the tagged protein (red) appeared to coincide with the parasite and/or the parasitophorous vacuole (cgd8_3560, Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: Upon infection with parasites tagged at the MEDLE2 locus, HCT-8 cells showed HA staining in the cytosol.
source: In contrast, upon infection with parasites tagged in the MEDLE2 locus (cgd5_4590), HCT-8 cells showed HA staining in the cytosol (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The cells that stain for MEDLE2-HA were those that were infected with parasites.
source: We note that the cells that stain for HA (red) were those that were infected with parasites, labeled with Vicia villosa lectin (VVL, green), and conclude that MEDLE2-HA is exported by the parasite into the host cell during or following invasion.
evidence: This is based on co-localization analysis in immunofluorescence images.

claim: MEDLE2-HA is exported by the parasite into the host cell during or following invasion.
source: We note that the cells that stain for HA (red) were those that were infected with parasites, labeled with Vicia villosa lectin (VVL, green), and conclude that MEDLE2-HA is exported by the parasite into the host cell during or following invasion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data.

claim: MEDLE1 and MEDLE6 localized around the parasite as well as to the host cell cytoplasm, but expression and export was less than what was observed for MEDLE2.
source: In IFAs, both tagged MEDLE1 and MEDLE6 localized around the parasite, as well as to the host cell cytoplasm, but expression and export was less than what was observed for MEDLE2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence imaging data.

claim: A chimeric mutant carrying an extra copy of MEDLE1-HA driven by the MEDLE2 promoter showed increased MEDLE1 expression making export into the host cell easier to appreciate.
source: To explore this difference, we engineered a chimeric mutant carrying an extra copy of MEDLE1-HA driven by the MEDLE2 promoter. Upon infection with these parasites, we observed increased MEDLE1 expression making export into the host cell easier to appreciate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is experimental data from a promoter swap experiment.

claim: Multiple members of the MEDLE family are host-targeted proteins.
source: We conclude that multiple members of the MEDLE family are host-targeted proteins.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the localization data for MEDLE1, MEDLE2, and MEDLE6.

claim: MEDLE2 was expressed and exported most robustly among the MEDLE family members tested.
source: Of these, MEDLE2 was expressed and exported most robustly and was selected for further study.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of the immunofluorescence data.

claim: MEDLE2 was observed at all time points during a 72 hr infection time course in HCT-8 cultures.
source: MEDLE2 was observed at all time points (Figure 2A) and quantification showed that the number of HA positive host cells (Figure 2B, red) increased over time, closely matching the increase in the number of parasites (blue).
evidence: This is based on time-course immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The number of MEDLE2-HA positive host cells increased over time, closely matching the increase in the number of parasites.
source: MEDLE2 was observed at all time points (Figure 2A) and quantification showed that the number of HA positive host cells (Figure 2B, red) increased over time, closely matching the increase in the number of parasites (blue).
evidence: This is based on quantification of time-course data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 94 ± 1.83% (mean ± SD, n = 3695) of the cells showing HA staining also showed parasite infection.
source: 94 ± 1.83% (mean ± SD, n = 3695) of the cells showing HA staining also showed parasite infection.
evidence: This is quantitative data from the time-course experiment.

claim: The high level of correlation between host cell HA expression and infection (r2 = 0.9) remained constant over 72 hr.
source: Importantly, this high level of correlation between host cell HA expression and infection (r2 = 0.9) remained constant over 72 hr.
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the time-course data.

claim: Previous work has shown synchronous life cycle progression in C. parvum cultures over 72 hours, with asexual stages initially replicating by merogony followed by a dramatic development switch at 40 hr to male and female gametes.
source: Previous work has shown synchronous life cycle progression over this time span. Initially, all parasites represent asexual stages replicating by merogony followed by a dramatic development switch at 40 hr, and later cultures are dominated by male and female gametes (Tandel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on a cited study on parasite life cycle staging.

claim: Host cells infected with female gametes and male gamonts at 48 hr were positive for MEDLE2-HA.
source: We staged parasites at 48 hr and identified female gametes and male gamonts using antibodies for the markers COWP1 and tubulin, respectively. We found the host cells infected with all these stages to be positive for MEDLE2-HA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on stage-specific immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MEDLE2 was exported to infected cells in vivo in Ifng-/- mice and exhibited cytoplasmic localization.
source: As shown by immunohistochemistry of sections of infected intestines in Figure 2E, MEDLE2 was exported to infected cells in vivo and exhibited cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data from infected mouse intestines shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MEDLE2 is not prepackaged into secretory organelles of sporozoites.
source: We readily observed labeling for the sporozoite antigen Cp23 but did not detect any HA staining in transgenic sporozoites, indicating that MEDLE2 is not prepackaged into secretory organelles (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence of sporozoites shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 4 hr post-invasion, MEDLE2-HA is first detectable with labeling being associated with the parasite.
source: At 4 hr, HA is first detectable, with labeling being associated with the parasite (parasite nuclei stained with Hoechst highlighted by white arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on time-course immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Beginning at 5.5 hr post-invasion, MEDLE2-HA staining was observed throughout the host cell cytoplasm and continued to accumulate over time.
source: Beginning at 5.5 hr, MEDLE2-HA staining was observed throughout the host cell cytoplasm and continued to accumulate over time (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on time-course immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MEDLE2 is predicted to be a 209 amino acid protein with a putative N-terminal signal peptide.
source: MEDLE2 is predicted to be a 209 amino acid protein with a putative N-terminal signal peptide suggesting trafficking through the parasite's secretory pathway.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction of the protein sequence.

claim: BFA treatment initiated after invasion ablated MEDLE2 export and resulted in the accumulation of MEDLE2-HA within the parasite.
source: BFA treatment initiated after invasion ablated export and resulted in the accumulation of MEDLE2-HA within the parasite (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on BFA treatment experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Image analysis and quantification showed the reduction in MEDLE2 export by BFA to be significant (p<0.0001).
source: Image analysis and quantification showed this reduction in export to be significant when comparing treated (red) to untreated cells (blue) (n = 98 treated; n = 198 untreated; p<0.0001; unpaired t test with Welch's correction; Figure 3E).
evidence: This is statistical analysis of the BFA treatment data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MEDLE2 is not injected by the sporozoite during invasion; rather, it is expressed and exported by the trophozoite and arrives in the host cell about 5 hr post infection.
source: We conclude that MEDLE2 is not injected by the sporozoite during invasion; rather, it is expressed and exported by the trophozoite and arrives in the host cell about 5 hr post infection (note that the length of the intracellular lytic cycle of asexual stages is 11.5 hr; Guérin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the timing experiments and BFA treatment data.

claim: Transgenic parasites expressing MEDLE2-mScarlet showed robust expression of the reporter when used to infect HCT-8 cultures, but fluorescence was associated with parasites, suggesting that MEDLE2-mScarlet remained trapped within or close to the parasite.
source: Transgenic parasites showed robust expression of the reporter when used to infect HCT-8 cultures. However, this fluorescence (red) was associated with parasites, highlighted by staining with VVL (Figure 4B, green), suggesting that MEDLE2-mScarlet remained trapped within or close to the parasite.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging of MEDLE2-mScarlet parasites shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cells infected with MEDLE2-BLA sporozoites accumulated CCF4-AM substrate but did not show substrate cleavage.
source: Cells infected with MEDLE2-BLA sporozoites were incubated with CCF4-AM, a cell-permeable substrate of beta-lactamase and imaged by live microscopy. Infected and uninfected cells accumulated CCF4-AM (Figure 4C, green); however, we did not detect substrate cleavage, resulting in blue fluorescence (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on live imaging of the beta-lactamase reporter assay shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MEDLE2-BLA was expressed but remained with the parasite.
source: To visualize localization of the MEDLE2-BLA fusion protein during infection, we performed IFA on MEDLE2-BLA-infected cells using a BLA antibody and observed that MEDLE2-BLA (green) was expressed but remained with the parasite (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, red).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cells infected with MEDLE2-Cre parasites remained green and did not show red fluorescence in the loxGFP/RFP color switch assay, despite robust infection.
source: Cells infected with either WT parasites or MEDLE2-Cre parasites remained green, despite robust infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multiple algorithms predict MEDLE2 to be a highly disordered protein.
source: We note that multiple algorithms predict MEDLE2 to be a highly disordered protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; low-complexity regions are indicated in light blue in Figure 5B) and conclude that translocation is blocked when folded reporters are fused to the protein.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Translocation of MEDLE2 is blocked when folded reporters are fused to the protein.
source: We note that multiple algorithms predict MEDLE2 to be a highly disordered protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 3; low-complexity regions are indicated in light blue in Figure 5B) and conclude that translocation is blocked when folded reporters are fused to the protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the failure of mScarlet, BLA, and Cre fusions to export.

claim: Removal of the sequence encoding the N-terminal signal peptide (ΔSP) prevented MEDLE2-HA export, and the resulting protein accumulated within the parasite.
source: Removal of the sequence encoding the N-terminal signal peptide (ΔSP) prevented MEDLE2-HA export, and the resulting protein accumulated within the parasite (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data of the ΔSP mutant shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When the KDVSLI motif was changed to six alanines, HA staining accumulated in the parasite and host cell staining was lost.
source: In contrast, when the most N-terminal sequence KDVSLI was changed to six alanines, HA staining accumulated in the parasite and host cell staining was lost (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data of the KDVSLI/6A mutant shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutation of residue leucine 35 to alanine (L35A) ablated MEDLE2 export and MEDLE2-HA remained with the parasite.
source: Mutation of residue leucine 35 to alanine (L35A) ablated export and instead MEDLE2-HA remained with the parasite (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data of the L35A mutant shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Changing the remaining five amino acids of the KDVSLI motif individually did not alter MEDLE2 localization in the host cell.
source: Changing the remaining five amino acids individually did not alter MEDLE2 localization in the host cell (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data of individual point mutants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Leucine 35 is critical for MEDLE2 export.
source: We conclude leucine 35 to be critical for export.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mutational analysis.

claim: For wild-type MEDLE2-HA, western blot analysis observed a single band with an apparent molecular weight of 31 kDa.
source: For WT MEDLE2-HA, we observed a single band with an apparent molecular weight of 31 kDa (Figure 5E, the predicted molecular weight for full-length MEDLE2-HA is 26.9 kDa but the abundance of positive charges is likely to result in reduced electrophoretic mobility).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The KDVSLI/6A mutant, which is no longer exported, appeared to be of a larger molecular weight than wild-type MEDLE2-HA.
source: In contrast, the KDVSLI/6A mutant, which is no longer exported, appeared to be of a larger molecular weight (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The mutant lacking the 22 amino acid signal peptide (ΔSP) produced an intermediate size band larger than the exported WT but smaller than the retained ΔKDVSLI mutant.
source: The mutant lacking the 22 amino acid signal peptide (ΔSP) produced an intermediate size band larger than the exported WT but smaller than the retained ΔKDVSLI mutant.
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The L35A mutation caused the mutant protein to migrate more slowly when compared to WT or the ΔSP mutant.
source: We found a very similar pattern when analyzing the single amino acid mutants, where the L35A change caused the mutant protein to migrate more slowly when compared to WT or the ΔSP mutant (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: When MEDLE2 wild-type and mutants are expressed in mammalian cells, the proteins are the same size.
source: To ensure the observed differences in apparent molecular weight were due to processing by the parasite and not the consequence of folding or subsequent host processing, we also expressed WT and mutants in mammalian cells (see Materials and methods for detail). In this context, the proteins are the same size (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on western blot data from mammalian cell expression shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The relative sizes of the mutated MEDLE2 proteins indicate processing at a point beyond the signal peptide, consistent with leucine 35.
source: Overall, we interpret the relative sizes of the mutated proteins to indicate processing of MEDLE2 at a point beyond the signal peptide, a position that would be consistent with leucine 35.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the western blot data.

claim: Processing of MEDLE2 at L35 appears to require translocation into the ER as it does not occur in mutants lacking a signal peptide.
source: We note that this processing appears to require translocation into the ER as it does not occur in mutants lacking a signal peptide.
evidence: This is an inference from the western blot data showing the ΔSP mutant has a different size.

claim: The L35A mutation apparently prevented removal of the signal peptide, suggesting that processing at L35 could replace the canonical signal peptidase activity.
source: Furthermore, the L35A mutation apparently prevented removal of the signal peptide, suggesting that processing at L35 could replace the canonical signal peptidase activity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the western blot data.

claim: Transfection of HEK293T cells with MEDLE2-GFP resulted in cytoplasmatic green fluorescence in roughly 40% of cells 24 hr post transfection.
source: Transfection with both constructs resulted in cytoplasmatic green fluorescence in roughly 40% of cells 24 hr post transfection (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on fluorescence imaging of transfected cells shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis of MEDLE2-GFP expressing cells versus GFP-only expressing cells revealed 413 upregulated genes and 487 genes with lower transcript abundance (adjusted p-value < 0.05).
source: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 413 upregulated genes and 487 genes with lower transcript abundance in MEDLE2-GFP-expressing cells compared to cells expressing GFP alone, with an adjusted p-value less than 0.05 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis detected changes in multiple pathways following introduction of MEDLE2 to host cells, with many converging upon translation, ribosomes, amino acid metabolism, and associated signaling.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) detected changes in multiple pathways following introduction of MEDLE2 to host cells (Figure 6—source data 1). Notably, many of these pathways converged upon translation, ribosomes, amino acid metabolism, and associated signaling (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the RNA sequencing data.

claim: Functional annotation clustering using DAVID of the GSEA results revealed multiple responses contributing to ER stress, including changes in genes linked to the unfolded protein response.
source: Functional annotation clustering using the Database for Annotation, Visualization and Integrated Discovery (DAVID) of the GSEA results revealed multiple responses contributing to ER stress, including changes in genes linked to the unfolded protein response (UPR).
evidence: This is based on functional annotation analysis of the GSEA results.

claim: The MEDLE2 response signature from transfected cells was enriched in a published dataset from C. parvum infection of a homeostatic mini-intestine model.
source: We next sought to explore whether the MEDLE2 gene signature observed following cell transfection was also present during Cryptosporidium infection using a published mRNA sequencing dataset generated from C. parvum infection of a homeostatic mini-intestine model (Nikolaev et al., 2020). We found enrichment for this MEDLE2 response signature with 51 genes of the MEDLE2 response present, and 22 of them contributing to the core enrichment of this response (Figure 6E, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of published infection data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: qPCR on ileal segments from C. parvum-infected mice showed that three of four ER stress response genes (NUPR1, CHAC1, DDIT3) were upregulated compared to uninfected controls.
source: As further validation that ER stress responses also occur during in vivo infection, we performed qPCR on ileal segments resected from mice infected with C. parvum or those that were uninfected. We measured the RNA abundance for the four genes highlighted in the volcano plot and found three to be upregulated in infected mice compared to uninfected controls (NUPR1, CHAC1, DDIT3, Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from infected mice shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Inhibition of the IRE1 signaling pathway with KIRA6 significantly reduced C. parvum parasite growth in HCT-8 cultures.
source: After 24 hr, cultures treated with KIRA6 showed reduced parasite growth when compared to the DMSO vehicle control (one-way ANOVA, Dunnett's multiple comparisons test p=0.0303).
evidence: This is based on nanoluciferase assay data from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Thapsigargin and GSK2606414 treatment did not affect C. parvum parasite growth in HCT-8 cultures.
source: Thapsigargin and GSK2606414 treatment did not affect parasite growth (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is based on nanoluciferase assay data from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 6G.

claim: C. parvum infection of Ddit3-/- mice resulted in a 56% reduction in the area under the curve compared to infection in C57BL/6J control mice.
source: C. parvum infection of Ddit3-/- mice resulted in a 56% reduction in the area under the curve compared to infection in C57BL/6J control mice (3,189,123 ± 69,887, 1,416,227 ± 44,850; total peak area ± standard error; unpaired t test, p<0.001; Figure 6H).
evidence: This is based on fecal luminescence data from infected knockout mice shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The ER stress response triggered by ectopic expression of MEDLE2 in mammalian cells is also observed during parasite infection in culture and mice and may contribute to parasite survival.
source: Taken together, the ER stress response triggered by ectopic expression of MEDLE2 in mammalian cells is also observed during parasite infection in culture and mice and may contribute to parasite survival.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective data on ER stress responses.

claim: The genomes of Cryptosporidium parasites reflect a high degree of similarity in conservation of gene content and synteny.
source: The genomes of these parasites reflect the overall high degree of similarity in their conservation of gene content and synteny; nonetheless, these parasites show pronounced differences in their host specificity (Feng et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited comparative genomic studies.

claim: Cryptosporidium parasites show pronounced differences in their host specificity despite genomic similarity.
source: The genomes of these parasites reflect the overall high degree of similarity in their conservation of gene content and synteny; nonetheless, these parasites show pronounced differences in their host specificity (Feng et al., 2017; Feng et al., 2018; Nader et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited comparative genomic studies.

claim: The genomic differences observed in Cryptosporidium are focused on families of predicted secretory proteins that have been proposed to contribute to host specificity, prominently among them the MEDLE family.
source: The genomic differences observed are focused on families of predicted secretory proteins that have been proposed to contribute to host specificity, prominently among them the MEDLE family (Fei et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Su et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on polymorphic gene families.

claim: Previous studies found that treatment of sporozoites with antisera raised against recombinant MEDLE1 or MEDLE2 diminished the efficiency of infection by 40%.
source: Previous studies found that treatment of sporozoites with antisera raised against recombinant MEDLE1 or MEDLE2 diminished the efficiency of infection by 40%.
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Previous authors considered that MEDLE proteins may play a role in invasion and that host specificity is rooted in receptor specificity.
source: This led the authors to consider that MEDLE proteins may play a role in invasion and that host specificity is rooted in receptor specificity (Fei et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of previous interpretations from cited studies.

claim: The timing of MEDLE2 expression and export and its sensitivity to BFA treatment argues for a mechanism that becomes active after the parasite has established its intracellular niche.
source: The timing of MEDLE2 expression and export and its sensitivity to BFA treatment argues for a mechanism that becomes active after the parasite has established its intracellular niche, in contrast to injection during invasion from organelles already poised to secrete.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on timing and BFA sensitivity.

claim: In P. falciparum, protein export relies on the translocon complex PTEX which uses the ATPase activity of a heat shock protein to unfold and then extrude cargo through a transmembrane channel into the red blood cell.
source: In P. falciparum, such export relies on the translocon complex PTEX (de Koning-Ward et al., 2009), which uses the ATPase activity of a heat shock protein to unfold and then extrude cargo through a transmembrane channel into the red blood cell (Ho et al., 2018; Matthews et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on P. falciparum protein export.

claim: Genetic ablation of the PTEX complex in P. falciparum results in loss of export and loss of parasite viability.
source: Genetic ablation of this complex results in loss of export and loss of parasite viability (Beck et al., 2014; Elsworth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited genetic studies on P. falciparum.

claim: In T. gondii, proteins are exported during intracellular growth via the MYR complex, which is independent of ATP hydrolysis and requires intrinsically disordered cargo.
source: In T. gondii, proteins are exported during intracellular growth via the MYR complex, which is independent of ATP hydrolysis and requires intrinsically disordered cargo (Hakimi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on T. gondii protein export.

claim: The T. gondii translocon and export are dispensable for growth in culture, but loss profoundly impacts virulence in vivo.
source: Translocon and export are dispensable for growth of this parasite in culture, but loss profoundly impacts virulence in vivo (Hakimi et al., 2017; Marino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on T. gondii.

claim: Genome searches do not readily identify C. parvum homologs of the components that make up the PTEX or MYR translocons, with the exception of a putative HSP101 chaperone.
source: With the exception of a putative HSP101 chaperone, genome searches do not readily identify C. parvum homologs of the components that make up these two previously characterized translocons (Pellé et al., 2015), but nonetheless, there are important parallels that suggest conserved features of Apicomplexan export.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and a cited reference.

claim: Disorder may be critical for MEDLE2 export as fusion of well-folded domains potently blocked its export into the host cell.
source: Disorder may be critical for MEDLE2 export as fusion of well-folded domains potently blocked its export into the host cell.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reporter fusion experiments.

claim: The requirement for disorder in MEDLE2 export is consistent with an export mechanism unable to unfold proteins as proposed for T. gondii and Plasmodium liver stages.
source: This is consistent with an export mechanism unable to unfold proteins as proposed for T. gondii and Plasmodium liver stages (Beck and Ho, 2021; Gehde et al., 2009; Marino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited studies on other Apicomplexan parasites.

claim: Export of proteins in P. falciparum and T. gondii requires a host-targeting motif that shares a required leucine residue linked to processing by an aspartyl protease.
source: Export of proteins in P. falciparum and T. gondii similarly requires a host-targeting motif (Coffey et al., 2015; Hiller et al., 2004; Marti et al., 2004). While the sequence of the motifs varies between species, all share a required leucine residue that has been linked to processing by an aspartyl protease to license export (Boddey et al., 2010; Coffey et al., 2015; Hammoudi et al., 2015; Russo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on P. falciparum and T. gondii.

claim: The aspartyl protease that processes exported proteins localizes to the ER in P. falciparum where it appears to replace the activity of signal peptidase.
source: This protease localizes to the ER in P. falciparum where it appears to replace the activity of signal peptidase for exported proteins, while the T. gondii homolog acts in the Golgi (Coffey et al., 2015; Marapana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on P. falciparum.

claim: The T. gondii aspartyl protease homolog acts in the Golgi.
source: This protease localizes to the ER in P. falciparum where it appears to replace the activity of signal peptidase for exported proteins, while the T. gondii homolog acts in the Golgi (Coffey et al., 2015; Marapana et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on T. gondii.

claim: Mutational analysis in C. parvum suggests that cleavage of L35 could replace the activity of signal peptidase similar to P. falciparum.
source: Our mutational analysis in C. parvum suggests that cleavage of L35 could replace the activity of signal peptidase similar to P. falciparum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mutational and western blot data.

claim: The C. parvum genome encodes six putative aspartyl proteases, three of which share significant similarity with the Plasmepsin V/ASP5 enzymes responsible for processing exported proteins in P. falciparum and T. gondii.
source: The C. parvum genome encodes six putative aspartyl proteases, three of which share significant similarity with the Plasmepsin V/ASP5 enzymes responsible for processing exported proteins in P. falciparum and T. gondii.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the C. parvum genome.

claim: Ablating the putative aspartyl protease genes in C. parvum may provide an opportunity to block export to the host cell.
source: Ablating these genes may provide an opportunity to block export to the host cell.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future experiments.

claim: Transient transfection of MEDLE2 into mammalian cells revealed a transcriptional signature of ER stress and UPR.
source: Here, we have identified the first examples of host-targeted effector proteins for intracellular stages of C. parvum. We introduced the protein into its target compartment, the mammalian cytosol, by transient transfection, and mRNA sequencing revealed a transcriptional signature of ER stress and UPR upon expression of MEDLE2, but not in matched control transfection with a GFP-only-expressing plasmid.
evidence: This is based on RNA sequencing data from transfected cells.

claim: An ER stress response signature was detectable when cells or mice were infected with C. parvum, which supports previous work identifying a UPR response during C. parvum infection in an in vitro model.
source: We found that an ER stress response signature was also detectable when cells or mice were infected with C. parvum, which supports previous work identifying a UPR response during C. parvum infection in an in vitro model of infection (Morada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of infection datasets and qPCR from infected mice, with support from a cited study.

claim: ER stress is a common feature of intracellular infection that greatly modulates host cell survival and inflammatory response.
source: ER stress is a common feature of intracellular infection that greatly modulates host cell survival and inflammatory response.
evidence: This is general knowledge in the field of host-pathogen interactions.

claim: Bacteria, viruses, and protozoa have evolved strategies to trigger or block the UPR during infection, suggesting the response is an active participant rather than a by-product of infection.
source: Bacteria, viruses, and protozoa alike have evolved strategies to trigger or block the UPR during infection, suggesting the response not to be a by-product of infection, but rather an active participant (Abhishek et al., 2018; Alshareef et al., 2021; Perera et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited reviews on pathogen-UPR interactions.

claim: Modulating the UPR is pivotal for intracellular bacteria that reside in vacuoles, including Chlamydia, Brucella, Listeria, and Mycobacterium, to build their intracellular niche and to acquire nutrients.
source: Modulating the UPR is pivotal for intracellular bacteria that reside in vacuoles, including Chlamydia, Brucella, Listeria, and Mycobacterium, to build their intracellular niche and to acquire nutrients (Celli and Tsolis, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited review on bacterial pathogens.

claim: Cryptosporidium lost the ability to synthesize most required metabolites and depends on an elaborate membranous feeder organelle at the host-parasite interface.
source: Cryptosporidium lost the ability to synthesize most required metabolites and depends on an elaborate membranous feeder organelle at the host-parasite interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Cryptosporidium metabolism.

claim: Cryptosporidium's metabolic reduction includes biosynthesis of many lipids.
source: This reduction includes biosynthesis of many lipids (Coppens, 2013), and we note modulation of lipid synthesis and mobilization as one important consequence of the UPR (Moncan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on Cryptosporidium metabolism and UPR effects.

claim: The UPR is important in the context of recognition of intracellular pathogens and the subsequent cytokine-mediated immune responses.
source: The UPR is also important in the context of recognition of intracellular pathogens and the subsequent cytokine-mediated immune responses.
evidence: This is general knowledge about UPR and immunity.

claim: Cryptosporidium triggers an enterocyte intrinsic inflammasome leading to the release of IL-18 from the infected cell.
source: Cryptosporidium triggers an enterocyte intrinsic inflammasome leading to the release of IL-18 from the infected cell (McNair et al., 2018), and infection also results in pronounced production of interferon λ (Ferguson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies on immune responses to Cryptosporidium.

claim: Cryptosporidium infection results in pronounced production of interferon λ.
source: Cryptosporidium triggers an enterocyte intrinsic inflammasome leading to the release of IL-18 from the infected cell (McNair et al., 2018), and infection also results in pronounced production of interferon λ (Ferguson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: GRA16, a disordered effector protein of T. gondii, similarly upregulates the ER stress response when tested in transfection experiments.
source: We also tested GRA16, a disordered effector protein of T. gondii in similar experiments and found it to similarly upregulate the ER stress response.
evidence: This is based on qPCR data from transfected cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The upregulation of ER stress response by disordered proteins may indicate that such upregulation is inherent to the structure of these proteins.
source: This may indicate that such upregulation is inherent to the structure of these proteins (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the comparative data.

claim: Manipulation of ER stress signaling using pharmacological inhibition of IRE1 in culture or genetic ablation of DDIT3 in mice resulted in reduced growth of C. parvum, suggesting that this response may contribute to parasite survival.
source: However, we note that manipulation of ER stress signaling using pharmacological inhibition of IRE1 in culture or genetic ablation of DDIT3 in mice resulted in reduced growth of C. parvum, suggesting that this response may contribute to parasite survival.
evidence: This is based on the drug treatment and knockout mouse experiments.

claim: MEDLE2 likely has additional roles yet to be determined beyond triggering ER stress.
source: We deem it likely that MEDLE2 has additional roles yet to be determined.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The MEDLE genes are highly polymorphic and encoded by multiple loci, but the current view of the family likely underestimates its true plasticity.
source: The MEDLE genes are highly polymorphic and encoded by multiple loci, but our current view of the family likely underestimates its true plasticity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the genomic complexity observed.

claim: Recent reannotation of the C. parvum genome using long read sequencing found evidence for multiple 'alternative' telomeres carrying different MEDLE gene clusters.
source: The recent reannotation of the C. parvum genome using long read sequencing found evidence for multiple 'alternative' telomeres carrying different MEDLE gene clusters (Baptista et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited genomic study.

claim: When the MEDLE2 gene was ablated by homologous recombination, additional MEDLE2 copies remained in the genome.
source: When we ablated the MEDLE2 gene by homologous recombination, additional MEDLE2 copies remained in the genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on PCR mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar observations of multiple gene copies were made when tagging the MEDLE2 gene.
source: Similar observations were made when tagging the gene (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on PCR mapping data.

claim: Cryptosporidium has a single host life cycle and undergoes sexual exchange throughout the infection, providing near constant opportunity for recombination.
source: It is important to note that Cryptosporidium has a single host life cycle and undergoes sexual exchange throughout the infection, providing near constant opportunity for recombination (Tandel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study on the parasite life cycle.

claim: The chromosomal organization of MEDLE genes is reminiscent of the importance of chromosomal position and recombination for the antigenically varied VSG and var genes in Trypanosoma brucei and P. falciparum, respectively.
source: This is reminiscent of the importance of chromosomal position and recombination for the antigenically varied VSG and var genes in Trypanosoma brucei and P. falciparum, respectively (Dreesen et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to cited studies on other pathogens.

claim: The fact that MEDLE proteins are delivered into the host cell makes them prime targets for immunity, and immune evasion may drive chromosomal organization, expression, and evolution of these genes.
source: The fact that MEDLE proteins are delivered into the host cell makes them prime targets for immunity, and immune evasion may drive chromosomal organization, expression, and evolution of these genes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation about the evolutionary implications of the findings.
